title: T2SCH31 Form (Schedule 31) - Canadian SR&ED Glossary
description: Learn how corporations use the T2SCH31 Form to calculate Canadian investment tax credits in our comprehensive SR&ED glossary.
summary: Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) is the form Canadian corporations file with Form T661 to claim federal SR&ED investment tax credits. It computes the 15% and 35% ITCs, applies the $6 million expenditure limit, calculates refundable amounts, tracks three-year carrybacks and 20-year carryforwards, and must be filed within 18 months of the taxation year-end.

It computes the 15% and 35% ITCs, applies the $6 million expenditure limit, calculates refundable amounts, tracks three-year carrybacks and 20-year carryforwards, and must be filed within 18 months of the taxation year-end.
Executive Summary and Statutory Architecture of Canadian R&D Incentives

Canada operates one of the most comprehensive and generous research and development (R&D) fiscal incentive regimes among industrialized nations, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Administered jointly through legislative policy formulated by the Department of Finance Canada and operational enforcement by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the SR&ED program distributes more than $4 billion annually in tax assistance to over 20,000 corporate and individual claimants across the country. Unlike discretionary direct grants that depend on competitive funding envelopes and ministerial pre-approval, the SR&ED regime is an entitlement framework embedded directly within the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and the Income Tax Regulations. When a taxpayer satisfies the statutory definitions of eligible scientific or technological work and incurs qualified expenditures within the prescribed statutory deadlines, the resulting tax deductions and Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) vest as a matter of statutory right.

The Canadian R&D tax architecture functions through a dual-benefit mechanism designed to address both multi-year tax liability management and immediate liquidity constraints for innovating enterprises. Under the first mechanism, governed by subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers may pool current—and, following recent legislative restorations, capital—SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada and deduct them in the current taxation year or carry them forward indefinitely to offset future business income. This statutory pooling mechanism expressly overrides the general capital and current deduction prohibitions contained in section 18 of the Income Tax Act. Under the second mechanism, governed by subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1) alongside section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, claimants earn federal ITCs ranging from a basic rate of 15% to an enhanced rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures. When stacked with provincial and territorial R&D tax credits—which provide an additional 3.5% to 30% in regional tax incentives—and direct innovation grants such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC-IRAP), Canadian enterprises can recover between 30% and 70% of their eligible R&D outlays.

Between 2024 and 2026, the federal and provincial R&D landscape underwent its most significant structural modernization in more than a decade. Culminating in federal legislation that received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, and took effect retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Parliament doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $6 million, expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historic $10 million to $50 million corridor to a substantially wider $15 million to $75 million corridor, extended the enhanced 35% credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored capital expenditures to SR&ED eligibility. Concurrently, Quebec enacted sweeping structural reforms in its 2025–2026 Budget Plan by introducing the consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation, and Commercialization (CRIC) and restoring capital asset eligibility for provincial purposes. These legislative shifts reflect a deliberate macroeconomic policy pivot toward retaining scale-up intellectual property and capital-intensive commercialization within Canada, counteracting long-standing structural criticisms from policy bodies and industry associations that the SR&ED program disproportionately favoured early-stage, labour-only small businesses while penalizing mid-market growth and domestic public capitalization.
Legislative Framework and the Statutory Definition of SR&ED
Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The legal gatekeeper for all federal and harmonized provincial R&D tax incentives is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set forth in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. For any technical activity to qualify, it must constitute a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The statute further bifurcates eligible investigation into three primary substantive streams alongside a fourth stream of enumerated supporting activities.

The first substantive stream, governed by paragraph 248(1)(a), encompasses basic research, which is defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. The second substantive stream, governed by paragraph 248(1)(b), encompasses applied research, which shares the requirement of advancing scientific knowledge but is undertaken with a specific practical application in view. The third and commercially predominant stream, governed by paragraph 248(1)(c), is experimental development, defined statutorily as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Across Canadian corporate tax filings, experimental development accounts for the overwhelming majority of industrial SR&ED claims, as it explicitly encompasses incremental technological improvements achieved in commercial engineering, manufacturing, and software environments.

Complementing these three core categories, paragraph 248(1)(d) extends SR&ED eligibility to eligible support work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs 248(1)(a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada. This statutory nexus ensures that routine technical activities—such as software coding, machining test fixtures, or running analytical assays—become eligible SR&ED activities when, and only to the extent that, they are necessitated by and directly serve to resolve an underlying scientific or technological uncertainty.

Conversely, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes several commercial, routine, and pre-production activities from qualifying as SR&ED, even if they require highly skilled scientists or engineers. Statutorily excluded activities encompass market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection. Where a project transitions from experimental verification into commercial production or routine debugging, the claimant must establish a clear technical and financial demarcation line so that excluded post-development costs are removed from the SR&ED claim.
The Intersection of Section 37 and Section 127

Once technical activities satisfy the threshold criteria of subsection 248(1), their financial treatment is governed by the statutory interplay of section 37 and section 127 of the Income Tax Act, alongside Part XXIX (specifically sections 2900 and 2902) of the Income Tax Regulations.

Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may deduct expenditures of a current nature under paragraph 37(1)(a)—as well as eligible capital expenditures following the 2024–2026 legislative restoration—incurred in the year on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly by the taxpayer or on the taxpayer's behalf. Expenditures accumulated in the subsection 37(1) pool do not expire; a corporate taxpayer may elect on line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1 to deduct all, part, or none of the available pool balance in a given taxation year, thereby preserving unused SR&ED deductions indefinitely to shelter taxable income in future profitable years.

Simultaneously, subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act defines a "qualified expenditure" for the purpose of computing the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit. While the subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base overlap substantially, they diverge in several critical respects. Most notably, when a taxpayer elects to use the Proxy Method under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) to (VI) to compute overhead, the resulting Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is included in "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) to generate ITCs, but is strictly excluded from the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool because the underlying overhead outlays are already deducted as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1). Similarly, while 100% of an eligible arm's-length Canadian subcontractor payment is deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool, only 80% of that contract payment qualifies for ITC calculation under subsection 127(9). Furthermore, under paragraph 12(1)(v) and paragraph 37(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act, any federal SR&ED ITC claimed by a taxpayer in a preceding taxation year—whether applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable or received as a cash refund—is recaptured into the tax base by reducing the subsection 37(1) deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year, and to the extent that the pool balance becomes negative, the excess is included directly in the taxpayer's business income under paragraph 12(1)(v).

body.text: Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Caps, Refundability, and the 2024–2026 Reforms
Evolution of the Enhanced and Basic Credit Tiers

The federal SR&ED regime stratifies claimants into two primary rate tiers: the enhanced 35% ITC rate—composed of the 15% basic rate under subsection 127(9) plus an additional 20% credit under subsection 127(10.1)—and the basic 15% ITC rate. Historically, the enhanced 35% rate was restricted exclusively to Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs, as defined in subsection 125(7) of the Income Tax Act) up to an annual qualified expenditure limit of $3 million. Under those legacy parameters, once a CCPC listed its shares on a public stock exchange, was acquired by foreign shareholders, or surpassed $50 million in prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada, its SR&ED credit rate dropped precipitously from a 35% fully refundable credit to a 15% non-refundable tax credit.

Recognizing that this sharp binary cliff discouraged domestic initial public offerings (IPOs) and eroded the global competitiveness of capital-intensive Canadian scale-ups, Parliament enacted major legislative amendments that received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, applying retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. While the CRA is actively updating its administrative forms and policy manuals to reflect Royal Assent, claimants are entitled to apply these enhanced statutory parameters for all qualifying taxation years.
Doubling of the Expenditure Limit and the Revised Taxable Capital Taper

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit eligible for the 35% enhanced ITC rate doubled from $3 million to $6 million. Consequently, the maximum annual federal cash refund available at the 35% rate on current expenditures doubled from $1.05 million to $2.1 million.

Simultaneously, subsection 127(10.2) of the Income Tax Act was amended to raise the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out thresholds from the previous $10 million to $50 million corridor to a significantly broader $15 million to $75 million corridor. Under the updated statutory formula in subsection 127(10.2), a CCPC's annual expenditure limit for a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024, is computed as follows:

Within this statutory equation, the variable A equals nil ($0) if the corporation's taxable capital employed in Canada (within the meaning assigned by section 181.2 or 181.3) for the immediately preceding taxation year, combined with the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of all associated CCPCs, is $15,000,000 or less. Where the combined prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, the variable A equals the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that combined prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000. Consequently, for every $10,000 of prior-year taxable capital above $15 million, the $6 million expenditure limit is reduced by $1,000, reaching zero precisely when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada reaches $75 million.

A critical technical nuance of the current subsection 127(10.2) formula is that prior-year taxable income no longer reduces the SR&ED expenditure limit. Although older administrative commentary and pre-2019 statutory provisions reduced a CCPC's expenditure limit when its prior-year taxable income exceeded $500,000, the modern statutory formula in subsection 127(10.2) tapers the $6 million expenditure limit solely by reference to prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (unless the corporation elects the revenue-based alternative under subsection 127(10.31)). Nevertheless, prior-year taxable income remains legally operative under subsection 127.1(2) for determining whether a CCPC constitutes a "qualifying corporation" eligible for 40% refundability on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures exceeding its expenditure limit: a "qualifying corporation" is defined as a CCPC whose taxable income for the previous taxation year, together with that of all associated corporations, did not exceed its qualifying income limit of $500,000, which is itself reduced as prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15 million.

body.text: Extension to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and the Revenue Election

A transformative pillar of the 2024–2026 legislative reform package is the introduction of the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) definition in subsection 127(9) alongside consolidated corporate group rules in subsection 127(10.62), which cross-reference the definition of "consolidated financial statements" in subsection 233.8(1) of the Income Tax Act. Under these provisions, qualifying Canadian-resident public corporations whose shares are listed on a designated stock exchange and that are not controlled directly or indirectly by non-residents can now earn the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on up to $6 million of qualified SR&ED expenditures annually. Because public corporations frequently maintain balance sheets that differ structurally from private corporations, an ECPC's $6 million expenditure limit is phased out based on its average annual revenue over the three preceding taxation years—derived from its consolidated financial statements where applicable under subsection 127(10.62)—rather than taxable capital employed in Canada.

Furthermore, under newly enacted subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) of the Income Tax Act, a CCPC may formally elect to have its expenditure limit determined using the ECPC three-year average annual revenue formula instead of the standard subsection 127(10.2) taxable capital formula. This revenue-based election creates a vital tax-planning mechanism for capital-intensive, asset-heavy CCPCs—such as clean-technology manufacturers, semiconductor or hardware ventures, and clinical-stage biotechnology enterprises—whose balance-sheet taxable capital exceeds $15 million due to substantial equity or debt financing of physical plant and equipment, but whose pre-commercial revenue remains minimal. By filing an election under subsection 127(10.31), an asset-heavy CCPC can preserve its full $6 million expenditure limit and $2.1 million refundable ITC despite holding between $15 million and $75 million in taxable capital employed in Canada.
Associated Corporations, Short Taxation Years, and Carryover Mechanics

Where a CCPC is associated with one or more other CCPCs in a taxation year within the meaning of section 256 of the Income Tax Act, subsection 127(10.21) mandates that the associated group share a single $6 million expenditure limit, which is tapered according to the combined prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of all CCPCs in the associated group under subsection 127(10.3). Pursuant to subsection 127(10.21), the expenditure limit of each individual associated corporation is statutorily deemed to be nil unless the corporations file an allocation agreement in prescribed form—Schedule 49—assigning the group's available expenditure limit among its constituent members. If the associated group fails to file a valid allocation agreement, the Minister of National Revenue is empowered under subsection 127(10.4) to allocate the expenditure limit among the associated corporations. Specific statutory relief and anti-avoidance provisions governing the deemed non-association of corporations are further set out in subsections 127(10.22) and 127(10.23).

Additionally, under subsection 127(10.5) (specifically paragraph 127(10.5)(b)), if a corporation has a short taxation year of less than 51 weeks—such as upon initial incorporation, corporate amalgamation, or an acquisition of control triggering a deemed year-end—its expenditure limit for that short taxation year must be prorated by multiplying the otherwise determined expenditure limit by the ratio of the number of calendar days in the short taxation year to 365. For example, under the legacy $3 million limit illustrated in the CRA's Investment Tax Credit Policy, a 184-day taxation year running from July 1 to December 31 yielded a prorated expenditure limit of $1,512,329 ($3,000,000 × 184 ÷ 365), whereas under the current $6 million limit for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an equivalent 184-day taxation year yields a prorated expenditure limit of $3,024,658 ($6,000,000 × 184 ÷ 365).

body.text: Any SR&ED ITC that is not refunded in the taxation year may be applied under subsection 127(5) of the Income Tax Act to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable. Unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years to recover prior Part I income taxes paid or carried forward 20 taxation years to shelter future tax liabilities. Under subsection 127(5), any SR&ED ITC that is refunded to a claimant in the taxation year is statutorily deemed to have been applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in that year, ensuring that refunded credits simultaneously reduce the balance of ITCs available for carryforward or carryback.
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Overhead Calculation Methodologies
Eligible Expenditure Categories

To generate SR&ED tax deductions and investment tax credits, an expenditure must be incurred in respect of SR&ED carried on in Canada and satisfy the specific cost-eligibility rules prescribed in section 37 of the Income Tax Act and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations.
Salaries and Wages of Employees Directly Engaged in SR&ED

Internal labour costs typically represent the single largest component of a Canadian SR&ED claim. Under subsection 37(1) and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, eligible salaries or wages encompass regular gross wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave, and taxable benefits conferred under section 6 of the Income Tax Act, prorated strictly for the proportion of time each employee spends directly performing, supervising, or supporting eligible SR&ED activities in Canada. Conversely, employee stock option benefits conferred under section 7 of the Income Tax Act, retiring allowances, and shareholder dividends are completely excluded from qualifying SR&ED salaries and wages. Furthermore, claimants must adhere strictly to subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, which governs unpaid remuneration accrued at year-end: any salary, wage, or bonus accrued in a taxation year that remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of that taxation year is statutorily deemed not to have been incurred in the accrual year, and is instead deemed to be incurred only in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid, where it is reported on line 310 of Form T661.
Statutory Restrictions on Specified Employees

Stringent anti-avoidance caps apply to the remuneration of "specified employees," defined in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act as any employee who is a specified shareholder—owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or any related corporation—or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer. For a specified employee, remuneration based on profits and all bonuses are entirely disallowed as SR&ED expenditures. Moreover, the maximum total eligible SR&ED salary or wages that may be claimed for a specified employee is capped at 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) established under the Canada Pension Plan, prorated for the number of days in the taxation year and shared across all associated corporations employing that individual. When a claimant uses the Proxy Method and calculates the salary base for the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the includable salary of each specified employee is restricted even further to the lesser of the employee's directly engaged SR&ED salary, 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (computed prior to any SR&ED allocation and excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and section 6 or section 7 benefits), and the 2.5 times YMPE ceiling.
Materials Consumed or Transformed

Under paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Income Tax Regulations, claimants may include the cost of materials that are either consumed—meaning they are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless during experimental runs—or transformed—meaning they are physically integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom device during the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Eligible materials may be sourced from either Canadian or foreign suppliers, provided the physical consumption or transformation takes place within Canada. However, where transformed materials or experimental prototypes are subsequently sold commercially or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED recapture provisions in subsections 127(27) to (35) of the Income Tax Act claw back the previously claimed ITCs by adding the recaptured credit directly to the taxpayer's Part I tax payable.
Canadian Subcontractors and Third-Party Payments

Taxpayers may claim expenditures incurred for SR&ED performed on their behalf by Canadian-resident subcontractors, provided the underlying R&D work is physically carried out in Canada. While 100% of an eligible arm's-length Canadian subcontractor invoice is deductible in the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool, a statutory haircut enacted in the 2012 federal budget and effective since January 1, 2013, restricts the subsection 127(9) "qualified expenditure" inclusion to 80% of the amount of an arm's-length third-party contract. This 20% reduction removes the subcontractor's notional profit mark-up from the federal ITC base while ensuring the contracting company retains title to the intellectual property and the SR&ED claim. Similarly, third-party payments made in money or in kind to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D corporations for SR&ED carried on in Canada are eligible for inclusion (at 80% for federal ITC purposes) when the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the research in its business.
Restored Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures—including the acquisition of depreciable machinery, laboratory equipment, and capital lease outlays—were excluded from both section 37 SR&ED deductions and section 127 ITCs. Under the 2024–2026 federal legislative reforms (and mirrored in Quebec's 2025–2026 CRIC reforms), capital expenditures and lease costs have been restored to SR&ED eligibility. Under the restored federal rules, CCPCs and ECPCs earn the enhanced 35% ITC on qualified SR&ED capital expenditures within their $6 million expenditure limit, with 40% of the unclaimed balance of that 35% capital ITC being refundable in cash (an effective 14% immediate cash refund plus a 21% non-refundable tax credit carryforward), compared to 100% refundability on current SR&ED expenditures and the PPA.
Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method for Overhead Allocation

A foundational financial election in every Canadian SR&ED filing is the annual choice between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method for capturing overhead and indirect supporting expenditures. The claimant must elect one method for the entire taxation year on Form T661 when filing the claim; once filed for a given taxation year, the chosen method is irrevocable for that year, even if a subsequent audit or recalculation reveals that the alternative method would have yielded a higher tax credit.
The Proxy Method and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)

Governed by subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) to (VI) of the Income Tax Act and subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the Proxy Method eliminates the burdensome accounting requirement of tracking, itemizing, and proving incremental R&D overhead. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the eligible "salary base". Historically, the PPA rate stood at 65% for 2012 and prior years and 60% for 2013 before being permanently set at 55% effective January 1, 2014; the CRA formally updated its Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy on April 28, 2022, to remove legacy transitional rate formulas.

The salary base under the Proxy Method consists strictly of the portion of salaries and wages of employees who are "directly engaged" in SR&ED in Canada—encompassing hands-on experimentation, engineering analysis, direct first-line technical supervision, and eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support tasks—reduced by the specified employee limitations (75% of total salary and 2.5 times YMPE). Under the Proxy Method, the calculated PPA is included in "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) and earns federal and harmonized provincial ITCs at the exact same rate and refundability as direct current expenditures. However, the PPA cannot be added to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the actual overhead expenses that the PPA represents—such as shop supplies, utilities, office expenses, and the salaries of indirect administrative or support staff who are not "directly engaged" in hands-on SR&ED—are deducted as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1) of the Income Tax Act and cannot be claimed separately on Form T661.

Furthermore, subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations subjects the PPA to an Overall Cap to ensure that the notional proxy amount does not exceed the taxpayer's actual non-SR&ED business operating deductions for the year. The Overall Cap is calculated using the statutory formula:
Overall Cap = A − B − C

In this regulatory formula, A represents the total of all amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold), while B and C represent specific deductions identified by the Income Tax Regulations that must be backed out, including the SR&ED deduction claimed in the year on line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1, Capital Cost Allowance (CCA), building rent, interest expenses, and other non-overhead deductions.
The Traditional Method

Governed by subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations, the Traditional Method requires the claimant to maintain a detailed, date-stamped cost-accounting system to identify, substantiate, and allocate actual overhead and other expenditures that are directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED. Specifically, under paragraph 2900(2)(c) and paragraph 2900(3)(b), claimed overhead expenditures must be directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED or to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED—meaning the claimant must prove that every dollar of claimed overhead would not have been incurred had the SR&ED activities not occurred. Under the Traditional Method, claimants may also include in the SR&ED pool and ITC base the salaries or wages of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support the performance of SR&ED even if their auxiliary support duties fall outside the narrower "directly engaged" salary base required by the Proxy Method.

body.text: As this structural comparison demonstrates, the Proxy Method maximizes the SR&ED claim and eliminates audit friction over overhead incrementality for the vast majority of software, engineering, biotechnology, and general manufacturing claimants whose actual incremental SR&ED overhead is less than 55% of direct non-specified SR&ED salaries. Conversely, the Traditional Method becomes financially superior when direct internal employee labour is low or zero—such as R&D programs executed predominantly by Canadian subcontractors or by specified employees whose salary base is severely compressed by the 75% and 2.5 times YMPE caps—or in large, capital-intensive industrial facilities where dedicated utilities, specialized plant supplies, and indirect support staff exceed 55% of direct hands-on wages.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Stacking Mechanics

Every Canadian province except Prince Edward Island, together with the Yukon territory, supplements the federal SR&ED program with regional R&D tax credits or innovation grants. With the exception of Quebec—which administers its fiscal incentives independently through Revenu Québec—and Alberta—which administers its Innovation Employment Grant through the Alberta corporate tax system—all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) through a unified corporate tax filing process on the T2 return and rely on the federal subsection 248(1) definition of eligible SR&ED work and qualified expenditure pools.
The Government Assistance Grind (Subsection 127(9))

A fundamental mathematical rule in Canadian R&D tax law is that all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and innovation grants constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act. Consequently, tax practitioners cannot simply add the headline federal credit percentage (35% or 15%) to the headline provincial credit percentage to compute the combined return. Instead, provincial R&D tax credits—as well as direct government grants or rebates such as NRC-IRAP or Save on Energy—must be deducted from the federal subsection 37(1) expenditure pool and the federal subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base before the federal ITC rate is applied.

Furthermore, when a claimant elects the Proxy Method, government assistance in the form of a general provincial R&D tax credit reduces the pool of actual allowable SR&ED expenditures, not the direct salary base used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (unless the assistance is specifically structured as a direct wage subsidy for an individual employee). Thus, if a corporation earns a harmonized provincial R&D tax credit at rate p on its total qualified expenditures (including the PPA in harmonized provinces like Ontario or British Columbia) and a federal ITC at rate f, the effective combined federal-provincial credit rate c on a given qualified expenditure base is governed by the equation:

For instance, for an Ontario CCPC qualifying for the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (p = 8%) and the 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITC (f = 35%) that waives the non-refundable ORDTC, every $100 of qualified expenditure (including the PPA) generates $8.00 of OITC, which grinds the federal qualified expenditure base down to $92.00; applying the 35% federal ITC to $92.00 yields $32.20, resulting in a combined cash refund of $40.20 (40.2%) on qualified expenditures, or 62.31% of direct SR&ED labour when multiplied by the 1.55 proxy factor (40.2% × 1.55).

Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, OBRITC, and the Strategic Waiver Election

Ontario operates a three-tier R&D tax credit system administered by the CRA for corporations maintaining a permanent establishment in Ontario. The primary small-business incentive is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 566, which provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit (reduced from 10% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) on up to $3 million of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures, yielding a maximum annual cash refund of $240,000. The OITC's $3 million expenditure limit is shared among associated corporations and gradually phases out when prior-year Ontario taxable income lies between $500,000 and $800,000 or when prior-year taxable paid-up capital lies between $25 million and $50 million.

The second tier is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508, which provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% after May 31, 2016) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures to all corporations regardless of size, with unused credits subject to a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward against Ontario corporate income tax. Crucially, the eligible expenditure base for the ORDTC must first be reduced by the dollar amount of any OITC and OBRITC claimed in the year. Because the ORDTC constitutes government assistance for federal SR&ED purposes, claiming a 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC automatically reduces the federal qualified expenditure base on which a CCPC earns a 35% refundable cash credit. For a pre-revenue or loss-making Ontario startup that has no Ontario corporate income tax payable, claiming the ORDTC reduces its immediate federal cash refund by 1.225% (3.5% × 35%) of its post-OITC expenditure base in exchange for a non-refundable carryforward credit. To prevent this cash erosion, Ontario tax legislation allows a corporation to formally waive the ORDTC in whole or in part by submitting a written waiver with its T2 return on or before six months after its taxation year-end (or on an amended return for that year), preserving 100% of its post-OITC expenditure base for the 35% federal cash refund.

The third tier is the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), claimed on Schedules 568 and 569, which provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with a designated Eligible Research Institute (ERI)—such as an Ontario university, college of applied arts and technology, hospital research institute, or designated non-profit research centre—up to a $20 million annual qualified expenditure cap ($4 million maximum annual refund) allocated across an associated group. To qualify, the corporate claimant must be entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED carried out under the agreement, and an anti-avoidance provision excludes any expenditure that may reasonably be considered to fund the salary or wages of an ERI employee who is connected to the claimant corporation.
Quebec: Independent Administration and the 2025–2026 CRIC Consolidation

Unlike the rest of Canada, Quebec administers its R&D tax incentives independently through Revenu Québec, requiring corporate claimants to file provincial CO-17 corporate tax returns and dedicated Revenu Québec R&D schedules separately from their federal CRA submission. Historically, Quebec's flagship R&D Salary Tax Credit provided a 100% refundable credit ranging from 14% to 30% on direct Quebec R&D salaries and 50% of eligible Quebec subcontractor and university research contract payments. Unlike the federal regime, Quebec does not apply a 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount; instead, Quebec applies higher nominal credit rates directly to eligible Quebec R&D labour and half of eligible contractor fees, subject to a statutory exclusion threshold ranging from $50,000 to $225,000 based on the corporation's prior-year total assets. Expenditures incurred below the exclusion threshold do not earn the Quebec R&D credit, though they remain fully eligible for the federal 35% or 15% SR&ED ITC.

In its 2025–2026 Budget Plan, the Quebec Ministère des Finances enacted a landmark structural reform by introducing the consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation, and Commercialization (CRIC). Under the CRIC regime, multiple legacy Quebec R&D tax credits were unified into a streamlined, 100% refundable credit providing an enhanced 30% refundable rate on the first $1 million of eligible R&D expenditures above the exclusion threshold for corporations of all sizes, and a 20% refundable rate (increased from the legacy 14% basic rate) on eligible expenditures exceeding $1 million. Mirroring the federal 2024–2026 reforms, Quebec's 2025–2026 Budget also restored the eligibility of capital expenditures used for R&D activities in Quebec. Additionally, the statutory rules were refined so that the calculation of the Quebec nexus ratio is not reduced by the CRIC exclusion threshold, while Revenu Québec updated its administrative guidance regarding institutional exclusions under criterion 5.
Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Atlantic Canada

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) applies to eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020, matching the federal SR&ED eligibility rules. The IEG provides qualified corporations with an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base spending level (the average of its eligible Alberta R&D expenditures over the two preceding taxation years) and an enhanced 20% refundable payment on incremental R&D spending exceeding that base level, up to an annual spending cap of $4 million. The statutory filing deadline for claiming the Alberta IEG is 15 months after the corporation's filing due date (21 months after year-end). In British Columbia, corporations claim the BC SR&ED Tax Credit via Form T666, which delivers a 10% fully refundable credit for CCPCs on up to $3 million (expanded up to $4 million in specific regional tiers) of qualified BC expenditures and a 10% non-refundable credit for non-CCPCs.

Meanwhile, Manitoba and the Atlantic Provinces offer exceptionally competitive incentives for large public or foreign-controlled enterprises conducting R&D in Canada. Whereas a large or foreign-owned corporation in Ontario earns only the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC alongside the 15% non-refundable federal ITC (for a combined rate of roughly 18.0%), Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Newfoundland and Labrador provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit with no expenditure cap to large and small corporations alike, and Manitoba provides a 15% R&D tax credit (changed from 20% after April 11, 2017) of which half (7.5%) is refundable in cash for in-house R&D and 100% is refundable for eligible research institute contracts. Consequently, a large enterprise conducting R&D in Manitoba or Atlantic Canada captures nearly double the combined federal-provincial credit value (~27.75% to 28.0%) compared to an equivalent large company operating in Ontario (~18.0%).
Governing Authorities, Filing Procedures, Deadlines, and CRA Audit Architecture
Required Tax Forms and Harmonized Filing Mechanics

To claim federal and CRA-administered provincial SR&ED tax incentives, a claimant must submit a synchronized technical and financial filing package with its annual income tax return. The cornerstone of every submission is Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim). Part 2 of Form T661 captures the technical project narratives demonstrating how the work satisfies the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) along with contemporaneous documentation indicators, while Parts 3, 4, and 5 quantify project-level costs, the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool, unpaid amounts governed by subsection 78(4) on line 310, and the Prescribed Proxy Amount calculation in Part 5.

Alongside Form T661, corporate claimants must file Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations)—while unincorporated individuals and trusts file Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals))—to compute the 15% and 35% federal ITCs, apply the $6 million expenditure limit formula, calculate refundable credit entitlements under section 127.1, and track 3-year carrybacks and 20-year carryforwards. Where a CCPC is associated with other corporations, the group must also file Schedule 49 to allocate the shared $6 million expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.21), and every corporate claimant reconciles its discretionary section 37 SR&ED pool deduction on line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1. Finally, applicable provincial schedules—such as Schedules 566, 508, 568, and 569 in Ontario, Form T666 in British Columbia, or Schedule 380 in Manitoba—are filed directly with the T2 return, whereas Quebec claimants submit Forms RD-222, RD-1029.7, and CRIC schedules with their CO-17 corporate return to Revenu Québec.
The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline

One of the most unforgiving procedural bars in Canadian tax administration is the SR&ED reporting deadline mandated by subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act. A taxpayer must file Form T661 and the corresponding ITC schedule (Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038-IND) containing all prescribed information in respect of an expenditure on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred.

Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act falls 6 months after the end of its taxation year, a corporate claimant has a total statutory window of exactly 18 months after the end of its taxation year to submit a complete SR&ED claim, whether filed with its original T2 return or via an amended filing. As policy reviews have noted, this 18-month post-year-end window allows retrospective claims for work initiated up to 2.5 years prior to the filing date (a 12-month taxation year plus 18 months). However, once the 18-month deadline expires, the statutory bar is absolute: the CRA possesses no administrative discretion under the taxpayer relief provisions of the Income Tax Act to accept a late-filed Form T661 or to allow expenditures omitted from Form T661 as of the 18-month cut-off date.
CRA Administrative Review and the "Why and How" Eligibility Guidelines

As outlined in the CRA's SR&ED Technical Review: A Guide for Claimants and the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, every SR&ED claim is initially screened upon filing at a CRA Tax Centre. Claims accepted as filed without audit are typically processed within 60 to 90 days, whereas claims selected for desk or field review require 90 to 180 days or several months depending on complexity. When a claim is selected for detailed review, it is routed to a Coordinating Tax Services Office (CTSO), where the CRA Control Centre assigns the file to a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), a Financial Reviewer (FR), or both.

During a detailed review, the RTA evaluates all technical information in the current and prior SR&ED filings, requests contemporaneous technical records, and—where a site visit or virtual interview is deemed necessary—provides the claimant with an advance list of activities and documents to be examined. At the conclusion of the site visit, the RTA is required by CRA procedure to provide the claimant with a preliminary verbal indication of eligibility decisions or outstanding concerns so the claimant has a fair opportunity to submit supplementary technical representations. The RTA then memorializes the technical determination in an SR&ED Review Report, which is combined with the Financial Reviewer's audit of labour, subcontractor, overhead, and PPA calculations into a joint CRA Proposal Letter before a formal Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued.

In 2021–2022, the CRA consolidated its administrative eligibility guidance into the simplified Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, which distil the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) and the five judicial questions from Northwest Hydraulic into two core requirements: the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement. Under the "Why" requirement, the claimant must demonstrate that the work was conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement—meaning the generation of new technological knowledge that resolves a system-level scientific or technological uncertainty that could not be removed through routine engineering or standard procedures known to competent professionals in the field. Under the "How" requirement, the claimant must demonstrate that the work was carried out as a systematic investigation or search by means of experiment or analysis—specifically by formulating explicit causal hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating the technological uncertainty, testing those hypotheses methodically, and maintaining contemporaneous records of the hypotheses tested and the experimental results as the work progressed. As the CRA explicitly emphasizes in its policy guidance, both the two requirements ("Why" and "How") and the five judicial questions derive directly from subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which did not change in law.
Landmark Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents

Because subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act employs broad statutory phrasing, the jurisprudence of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) serves as the binding legal authority governing SR&ED eligibility and evidentiary standards.
1. The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839, TCC) and CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393)

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, Chief Justice Donald Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada articulated the foundational judicial framework for interpreting subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Citing Conoltex Inc., Justice Bowman emphasized that Parliament enacted SR&ED tax incentives to encourage scientific research in Canada and that courts and tax administrators should interpret the legislation purposively to fulfil that objective. Justice Bowman set forth five criteria—subsequently endorsed and summarized as five formal questions by the Federal Court of Appeal in CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393—that a taxpayer must establish on a balance of probabilities:

First, was there a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? If the resolution of the technical problem is reasonably predictable using established methodologies and standard practice available to competent professionals in the field, the work constitutes routine engineering rather than SR&ED. Second, did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? This requires a five-step scientific methodology: observing the subject matter of the problem, formulating a clear objective, identifying and articulating the underlying technological uncertainty, formulating a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate that uncertainty, and methodically testing the hypotheses through experiment or analysis. Third, did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? Unstructured trial-and-error or intuitive debugging without causal hypotheses fails this third criterion. Fourth, did the process result in a technological advancement? A technological advancement represents an advancement in general technological understanding recognizable to skilled practitioners in the field, including incremental advancements or the scientific rejection of a hypothesis proving why a given technical approach fails under defined constraints. Fifth, although the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations do not expressly state that a claimant must keep detailed records, was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and the results, kept as the work progressed?
2. Mandatory Nature of the Scientific Method: Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 92)

In recent appellate litigation, several claimants argued that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria were merely judicial guidelines and that the third criterion—whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method—was not a strict statutory requirement under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, and again in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 92 (written by Justice Rennie and decided in May 2022), the Federal Court of Appeal decisively rejected this contention. The Federal Court of Appeal held that Kam-Press had settled the law by declaring that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria represent the authoritative and mandatory legal interpretation of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1). Where a trial judge finds on the evidentiary record that a claimant did not conduct its investigation in a methodical manner in accordance with the scientific method and failed to keep adequate records, the claim must be dismissed, and the exclusion of an expert report cannot cure an absence of primary factual evidence showing systematic experimentation. This strict adherence to the Northwest Hydraulic criteria echoes earlier Tax Court rulings such as Airmax Technologies Inc. and 2000 DTC 2353 (involving the KDS project), where appeals were dismissed because hypotheses were not formulated and record-keeping was inadequate.
3. Oral Testimony and Hypothesis Rejection: Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 48)

In Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 48, a Canadian food-manufacturing corporation appealed the Minister's disallowance of several SR&ED claims under paragraph 248(1)(c) involving novel food formulations and processing lines. Ruling in favour of the appellant taxpayer, the Tax Court of Canada held that the detailed, credible oral testimony of Canafric's CEO (Mr. Pandya), supported by existing operational records, satisfied all five Northwest Hydraulic questions. Crucially, the Tax Court reaffirmed that to satisfy the fourth criterion (technological advancement), a project does not need to achieve commercial success; rather, it must generate a technological advancement recognizable to experts in the field, which expressly includes the rejection of a hypothesis following systematic experimentation.
4. Contemporaneous Documentation vs. Substantive Proof: Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025 TCC)

In the recent landmark decision Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (allowing the taxpayer's appeal from a November 15, 2021 Notice of Assessment for the 2020 taxation year), the Tax Court of Canada clarified the evidentiary burden governing the first and fifth Northwest Hydraulic criteria. Regarding the first criterion (technological uncertainty), the Court emphasized that merely facing an uncertain path toward a commercial objective is not, in and of itself, sufficient to qualify a project as SR&ED; the taxpayer must prove on a balance of probabilities that the technical uncertainty could not be resolved through routine engineering or standard procedures. Regarding the fifth criterion (record-keeping), the Tax Court pushed back against rigid CRA audit demands for specialized documentation, holding that while contemporaneous documentation may be necessary to resolve factual disputes between the parties, "the existence of contemporaneous documentation, or contemporaneous documents with specific intent, is not a condition to the recognition of scientific research or experimental development" under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Consequently, where a taxpayer proves through credible witness testimony and ordinary operational records that systematic hypothesis testing took place, the CRA cannot deny the claim solely because documents were not created with the specific intent of documenting SR&ED.

body.text: Strategic Audit and Compliance Conclusions

The statutory and jurisprudential analysis of Canada's R&D tax framework yields several vital operational imperatives for corporate taxpayers, legal counsel, and tax auditors. First, following Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, mid-market CCPCs with taxable capital between $10 million and $75 million—as well as Eligible Canadian Public Corporations—must immediately re-evaluate their R&D tax posture. Asset-heavy CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15 million should model the subsection 127(10.31) revenue election to determine whether switching to the three-year average annual revenue test preserves a greater portion of the $6 million expenditure limit. Simultaneously, corporations acquiring laboratory equipment or production pilot machinery should track capital asset utilization against the 90% SR&ED threshold to capture the newly restored federal (35% rate, 40% refundable) and Quebec CRIC capital tax credits.

Second, corporate claimants must carefully model provincial stacking interactions and statutory waivers. In Ontario, startups and growth companies that do not anticipate owing Ontario corporate income tax in the near term should proactively file a written ORDTC waiver within six months of their taxation year-end so that the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC does not grind down their 35% federal cash refund. Conversely, multinational enterprises establishing domestic R&D centres for foreign-controlled or large public corporate structures should weigh the substantial refundable credit advantages offered by Quebec (under the consolidated 20% to 30% CRIC regime), Manitoba (15% credit, half refundable), and Atlantic Canada (15% fully refundable) against Ontario's 3.5% non-refundable tier.

Finally, on the compliance and audit front, while the Tax Court of Canada's rulings in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025 TCC) and Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 48) confirm that specialized SR&ED documentation is not a strict legal condition precedent when oral testimony and business records establish systematic experimentation, the Federal Court of Appeal's decisions in Kam-Press (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D Inc. (2022 FCA 92) prove that failing to adhere to the scientific method is fatal. Claimants should therefore embed the CRA's "Why" (technological uncertainty beyond routine engineering) and "How" (hypothesis formulation, experimental testing, and analysis) directly into their engineering workflows while strictly enforcing the 18-month filing deadline under subsection 37(11) and structuring specified employee compensation as regular base salary paid within 180 days of year-end under subsection 78(4).
